lesson.title: The Access Point: Where Wireless Meets Wired
lesson.summary: An access point is the device that lets Wi-Fi clients join a network by bridging the wireless medium to the wired infrastructure behind it, coordinating every station within its radio range.
lesson.body:
A wireless LAN needs some fixed point where the radio world and the wired world meet. Client devices, laptops, phones, and IoT sensors move around and come and go, but somewhere the data they send has to land on a stable, wired network so it can reach a router, a file server, or the internet. That fixed point is the access point, usually abbreviated AP: a device with a radio built to Wi-Fi, IEEE 802.11, specifications on one side and an Ethernet port on the other.

Functionally, an access point acts as a bridge, forwarding frames between the wireless medium and the wired distribution system, typically Ethernet, using the same MAC addressing and frame formats the Wi-Fi standard defines. Every AP has a MAC address, and in Wi-Fi terminology this address doubles as the BSSID, the identifier for the basic service set the AP creates and manages, a concept covered next. The AP also handles the coordination duties a shared wireless medium requires: broadcasting beacon frames so nearby devices know the network exists, authenticating and associating new clients, encrypting traffic when security is configured, and managing which clients get to transmit when.

In a home, the box people call the router is usually several devices in one enclosure: a router doing IP routing and address translation to the internet, a switch with a few Ethernet ports, and an access point providing Wi-Fi, all sharing one case and one power supply. In an office or a university building, these roles are commonly split apart: dedicated access points are mounted on ceilings throughout the building, each wired back with Ethernet to switches in a wiring closet, and a separate wireless controller centrally manages settings, channel assignments, and security policy across dozens or hundreds of individual APs.

Consider a three story office building with one access point on each floor, all wired into the same building network and all broadcasting the same network name. An employee's laptop on the second floor associates with the second floor AP. When that AP receives a wireless frame from the laptop destined for a printer on the wired network, it strips the 802.11 wireless framing, re-frames the data as ordinary Ethernet, and forwards it out its wired port toward the printer, reversing the process for replies heading back to the laptop. To the printer, the traffic looks like it came from any other device on the wired LAN; the wireless hop is invisible above the access point.

Because every associated client shares that one AP's radio and airtime, a single access point can only comfortably serve so many active devices before performance degrades for everyone, which is why buildings deploy many APs rather than one powerful one. How those associated clients organize under an AP, what identifies the network they are joining, and how multiple APs cooperate to look like one seamless network are exactly the ideas the SSID, BSS, and ESS concepts cover next.
